result.markdown: --- title: "Six-Sided Die" subtitle: "Discrete and flat, but perfectly symmetric" --- ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-summary="Show the simulation code"} source("../R/clt_functions.R") rgen <- function(n) sample(1:6, size = n, replace = TRUE) # n fair rolls mu <- 3.5 sigma <- sqrt(35 / 12) # = 1.708 pop_kurt <- -1.2686 # excess kurtosis of a fair die coarse <- c(1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 32, 34, 36, 38, 40, 45, 50, 60, 75, 100, 200) exper <- run_with_refinement(rgen, coarse, mu, sigma) res <- exper$results n_main <- smallest_normal_n(res) n_std <- n_by_standard(res) at <- function(k) res[res$n == k, ] save_results(res, "die") save_summary(res, "Six-sided die", n_main, prediction = "15", key_note = "Symmetric: flat shape and discreteness are the only obstacles") ``` ::: ::: {.answer-box} n = 8 under my main standard (strict standard: ≈ 38 · lenient standard: 3 · my prediction: 15) ::: ## 1. What population am I sampling from? A fair six-sided die: the values 1 to 6, each with probability 1/6. It is the opposite of a bell curve. It is **flat** (no peak), **bounded** (no extreme values at all), and **discrete** (only six possible values). It is, however, perfectly **symmetric**. | Property | Value | |---|---| | Mean μ | 3.5 | | Standard deviation σ | √(35/12) ≈ 1.708 | | Skewness | 0 (symmetric) | | Excess kurtosis | −1.27 (light tails: flat, no extremes) | | Theoretical SE of the mean | 1.708/√n | ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} style_par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1)) barplot(rep(1/6, 6), names.arg = 1:6, col = adjustcolor(pal$bars, 0.75), border = NA, ylim = c(0, 0.2), xlab = "Face", ylab = "Probability") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The population: six equally likely values.](02_die_files/figure-html/fig-population-1.png){#fig-population width=990} ::: ::: ## 2. What did I expect before running the simulation? > **n = 15.** The die is symmetric (skewness 0) but flat and discrete. In my pilot run it clearly failed > at n = 1 and passed every check at n = 15, so I predicted 15. ## 3. Which sample sizes did I investigate? 1. **Coarse grid:** n = 1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 32, 34, 36, 38, 40, 45, 50, 60, 75, 100, 200. It is denser between 30 and 50 to locate the strict standard. 2. **Refinement:** every n from 6 to 9. B = 100,000 sample means per n, seed 9426. For plotting, each histogram bar is one possible value of the mean. The average of n rolls can only be a multiple of 1/n, so there are 5n + 1 possible values. ## 4. Results ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot_convergence(res, chosen_n = n_main, theory_skew = 0, theory_kurt = pop_kurt) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The four checks. Skewness is zero from the start; the Q-Q correlation is the last check to pass. Orange: theoretical kurtosis −1.27/n.](02_die_files/figure-html/fig-convergence-1.png){#fig-convergence width=990} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} n_show <- c(1, 2, 3, 5, n_main, 30) plot_hist_grid(exper, n_show, mu, sigma, step = 1) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Sampling distribution of the mean of n rolls (one bar per possible value) and the CLT normal curve.](02_die_files/figure-html/fig-hist-1.png){#fig-hist width=990} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot_qq_grid(exper, n_show) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Q-Q plots. At small n the points form visible steps (discreteness) and an S-shape (light tails).](02_die_files/figure-html/fig-qq-1.png){#fig-qq width=990} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot_se_check(res) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Simulated SE (dots) against σ/√n (line).](02_die_files/figure-html/fig-se-1.png){#fig-se width=990} ::: ::: The simulated mean stayed within 0.0093 of 3.5, and the simulated SE was within 0.5% of σ/√n at every n. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Full results table ::: {#tbl-results .cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} | n| Mean (sim)| SE When did the sampling distribution become approximately normal? $$\boxed{n = 8}$$ ::: {#tbl-standards .cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} |Standard | Max |skewness|| Smallest n| |:----------------------|------------------------:|----------:| |Strict | 0.10| 38| |**Main (my standard)** | 0.25| **8**| |Lenient | 0.50| 3| ::: ::: ## 6. Why did I choose that value? - **Skewness never mattered.** It was -0.009 at n = 1 and stayed near zero, because the die is symmetric. - **The flat shape faded quickly.** Excess kurtosis follows −1.27/n and passed my ±0.5 limit at n = 3. - **The Q-Q correlation was the last check to pass**, at n = 8. At small n the Q-Q plot is a staircase with an S-shape: the steps come from discreteness, and the S comes from the missing tails (a sum of a few dice can never be very far from 3.5). - At **n = 8** all four checks pass: skewness -0.014, kurtosis -0.167, Q-Q r 0.9980, tails 2.44% / 2.30%. Every larger n also passes. Every tested sample size below this n fails at least one check. ## 7. What surprised me? > I expected the die to stay visibly discrete for a long time, since it only has six values. It passed > my main standard at n = 8. What surprised me more is that it also passed the strict standard > at around n = 38. Its skewness was zero from the start, so the only problems were the > flat shape and the gaps between possible values. With n rolls the mean can take 5n + 1 different values, > and by n = 40 the gaps are less than a tenth of a standard error. So even for a discrete distribution > like a die, a larger n improves the approximation quite well.
